person.name: Joseph_Weizenbaum
person.summary: Joseph Weizenbaum was a German-American computer scientist who created ELIZA, an early program for text conversation between people and computers. His alarm at users' responses to ELIZA led him to argue that humans must retain moral responsibility for consequential decisions.

conclusion: ELIZA is regarded as a prototype for modern chatbots. Computer Power and Human Reason argued that people must retain authority over moral decisions, even when computer systems provide information.

events.title: Birth in Berlin
events.description: Joseph Weizenbaum was born in Berlin to Jechiel Weizenbaum, a master furrier, and Henriette Weizenbaum. He grew up in their Jewish family with his brother Heinrich Weizenbaum. Heinrich later became a computer scientist and used the name Henry F. Sherwood in the United States.

events.title: Emigrates to America
events.description: In 1936 Joseph Weizenbaum left Bremen with his parents, Jechiel and Henriette Weizenbaum, for the United States. Nazi persecution had forced him from his Berlin secondary school into a Jewish boys' school.

events.title: Studies Mathematics in Detroit
events.description: Joseph Weizenbaum began studying mathematics at Wayne State University in Detroit, Michigan, in 1941. His university training began five years after his family reached the United States.

events.title: Serves in Army Weather
events.description: In 1942 Joseph Weizenbaum interrupted his mathematics studies at Wayne State University to serve in the meteorological division of the [[United States Army Air Forces]]. He served there during the Second World War.

United States Army Air Forces.explanation: The United States Army Air Forces was the aviation branch of the U.S. Army during World War II. Its meteorological division provided weather information for military operations.

events.title: Completes Master's Degree
events.description: Joseph Weizenbaum returned to Wayne State University in Detroit after military service in 1946. He completed a master's degree in mathematics in 1950. He then became a research assistant in the mathematics faculty and helped design, build, and operate a large computer.

events.title: Joins General Electric
events.description: Joseph Weizenbaum became a systems engineer at General Electric Corporation's Computer Development Laboratory in 1952. He worked on the design, construction, and operation of large computers. He also helped develop one of the first computer banking systems.

events.title: Joins the MIT Faculty
events.description: Joseph Weizenbaum joined the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge, Massachusetts, as an associate professor in 1963. MIT became the institution where he developed his work on computers and human responsibility.

events.title: Develops ELIZA at MIT
events.description: Joseph Weizenbaum began developing ELIZA at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge, Massachusetts, in 1964. He wrote it in [[SLIP|SLIP, a list-processing programming language]]. Its DOCTOR script imitated the responses of a [[Rogerian psychotherapy|Rogerian psychotherapist]].

SLIP.explanation: SLIP was Weizenbaum's programming language for manipulating lists of symbolic data. It provided the technical environment in which he wrote ELIZA.

Rogerian psychotherapy.explanation: Rogerian psychotherapy is a client-centered approach associated with psychologist Carl Rogers. It commonly uses reflective, non-directive responses to encourage the speaker to continue.

event_class.title: ELIZA
event_class.description: ELIZA matches words and sentence patterns in a user's text, then applies scripted transformations to generate an apparently conversational reply.
event_class.impact: Users often took ELIZA's simple replies seriously and disclosed intimate details during conversations with it.

events.background:
Interactive computing was still unfamiliar in the mid-1960s. A user at MIT communicated with the computer through a teletype, while the program ran on an IBM 7094 under the Compatible Time-Sharing System. Personal computers were still eleven years away from becoming familiar to the public. Systems that handled ordinary written language would not become common in online services for decades. ELIZA grew from an experiment in whether a machine could sustain an exchange that felt briefly like a conversation between two people.

Its design separated the general program from scripts that supplied the vocabulary and instructions for a particular style of exchange. The DOCTOR script avoided the need for a store of real-world facts. Its prompts could return parts of a user’s statement as a question, which kept the exchange moving. The script assigned priorities to keywords and used rules that turned a sentence containing one of them into a prepared form of reply. Changes to the active script could alter the program’s manner. The program could not acquire new words or speech patterns from a conversation on its own.

The name came from Eliza Doolittle in George Bernard Shaw’s Pygmalion, later adapted as the hit musical My Fair Lady. Weizenbaum associated the name with the fictional character’s incremental training in upper-class speech. Users could similarly revise the program a little at a time through its script. The comparison had a limit. Eliza Doolittle learned, while the program required direct editing for every added pattern.

The original MAD-SLIP source code disappeared for many years. Publishing source code alongside an article was uncommon in the 1960s. The code was later found in the MIT archives and made available through outlets including the Internet Archive. It preserves an early example of software layering, with the general conversation program kept apart from the language-specific instructions.

events.title: Publishes ELIZA Paper
events.description: Joseph Weizenbaum published a paper about ELIZA in 1966 while working at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge. It described [[natural language processing|how computers process human language]] through a conversation that remained superficial. ELIZA was celebrated as an achievement in artificial intelligence.

natural language processing.explanation: Natural language processing is the field of making computers analyze or generate human language. ELIZA was an early experiment in creating the appearance of a conversation.

event_class.title: ELIZA: A Computer Program for the Study of Natural Language Communication between Man and Machine
event_class.impact: The program draws attention from users and researchers who attribute understanding and feelings to its responses.

events.background:
Interactive computing through a teletype was still new at the time. ELIZA ran on MIT’s Compatible Time-Sharing System, which let people work with a central IBM 7094 computer through terminals. Personal computers would not become familiar to the general public for another 11 years. The program’s architecture separated its general conversation mechanism from the scripts that supplied its language rules. This allowed the same underlying program to take on different conversational roles.

The DOCTOR script drew on Rogerian psychotherapy, in which a therapist often reflects a patient’s words back to them. Its setting spared the program from needing a store of ordinary facts about the world. The script assigned priorities to keywords in a user’s text. It then used transformation rules to turn parts of that text into nondirective questions. The name ELIZA came from Eliza Doolittle in George Bernard Shaw’s Pygmalion. Weizenbaum associated the program’s capacity for incremental revision by users with Doolittle’s instruction in upper-class speech. The program itself could not acquire new words or speech patterns from a conversation. Someone had to edit the active script to alter its responses.

One encounter in Weizenbaum’s office became the best-known account of the program’s effect. His secretary asked him to leave the room so she could have a real conversation with ELIZA. He later wrote that brief exposure to a simple program could induce “powerful delusional thinking in quite normal people.” The original MAD-SLIP source code disappeared after the 1960s. Publishing an article with source code was uncommon at the time. The code was later found in the MIT archives and made available through outlets including the Internet Archive. It preserves an early example of organizing software in layers and abstractions.

At the 1972 International Conference on Computer Communication, ELIZA held a computer-only conversation with PARRY, a program designed to simulate a patient with schizophrenia.

events.title: Formulates the Weizenbaum Test
events.description: In 1972 Joseph Weizenbaum formulated questions later known as the Weizenbaum Test. The questions asked whether an artificial-intelligence application would benefit society and whether it should be built. He argued that computers could provide information while people retained authority over moral decisions.

events.title: Publishes Computer Power and Human Reason
events.description: Joseph Weizenbaum published Computer Power and Human Reason in 1976. The book argued that people must retain authority over moral decisions. It warned against assigning such judgments to computer systems.

images.caption: Computer Power and Human Reason by Joseph Weizenbaum
images.creator: NW7US

event_class.title: Computer Power and Human Reason: From Judgment to Calculation

events.title: Founds Social Responsibility Group
events.description: In 1983, Joseph Weizenbaum helped found Computer Professionals for Social Responsibility in the United States. The group brought computer professionals into discussions of the social and political consequences of computing.

events.title: Returns to Berlin
events.description: In 1996, Joseph Weizenbaum left the United States and returned to Berlin. He settled near one of his daughters and close to the former family apartment.

events.title: Receives Federal Cross
events.description: In 2001, Germany awarded Joseph Weizenbaum the Grand Cross of Merit of the Federal Republic of Germany. The honor recognized his public work on the social responsibilities of science and computer technology.

images.caption: Grand Cross of Merit with star and sash
images.creator: GrafVonEbbell

events.title: Appears in Rebel Film
events.description: In 2006, Joseph Weizenbaum appeared in the documentary Weizenbaum. Rebel at Work, directed by Peter Haas and Silvia Holzinger. He discussed ELIZA and argued that human beings should retain decision-making authority over computer systems.

events.title: Death in Berlin
events.description: Joseph Weizenbaum was diagnosed with cancer in 2007. Chemotherapy did not succeed. He died in Berlin on March 5, 2008, from complications of a stroke.
